chapter_theme: Podanam's king, hearing Asvagriva's demand for tribute, reasons from fate and precedent to submit and gives the envoys women and gifts, until Tivittan learns of it, flares at the word tribute and answers in scorn.

cast.role: the king of Podanam, called by the epithet of the swift elephants
the sceptre-bearing sky-goers sent by Asvagriva for tribute, the Vidyadharas of 678
the women of the hall, dancers and singers whom the king gives away
the red-eyed tall one, the younger prince and hero
the dwarf who tells the prince what has happened
the discus-lord, son of Mayurakandan and Nilanganai, whose demand brings the envoys

666.reading: The king, having heard the envoys' demand, keeps their angry words inside his mind as an elephant keeps a stone thrown by a vain man in its cheek, and turns to a mind that weighs gentle courses.
666.nuance: The simile is hard: the thrown stone and its being held in the cheek as if it were a scent-ball are read as swallowed insult; the verse does not say outright that the king hides his anger.
666.event: The king hears the demand and swallows the insult without showing it.

667.reading: The speaker says that, however a man's birth, learning and form stand, each is made to hear another's word, act on it and live by it by the lord called master of deeds.
667.nuance: The first three lines turn on a hard clause about baseness that cannot be blamed; the sense of the verse as a whole is held loosely. The king is taken as the one reflecting, from 671, where his thought is said to end.

claims.claim: a lord called master of deeds orders that men hear one another's word, act on it and so live

668.reading: The speaker says that men who plan to enjoy the wealth they gained with effort are weakened by fate, which upsets the city, takes what they hold and hands it to others, and no one can bar it.
668.nuance: Set beside 680 to 683, the king's fate-talk is a reason offered for giving way; the verse does not say that the loss has already come, only that fate can cause it.

claims.claim: fate takes what a man has gathered and gives it to others, and nothing can hold it back

669.reading: The speaker says that those who live by the favour of a man great in splendour sink in the wish to live by his grace, and though they see it plainly they do not weigh the workings of deeds.
669.nuance: The speaker takes the knowledge of deeds as the knowledge he and his own lack; the verse blames desire for favour, not the overlord.

claims.claim: those who live on a greater man's favour forget how deeds work

670.reading: The speaker says that since the deeds done earlier are of this kind, there is nothing to gain by fretting now, and that he has heard how the earlier kings of the sea-ringed earth joined and pleased the overlord and ruled.
670.nuance: This is where the king's reasoning from deeds becomes a decision: the fruit of deeds is read as a reason to pay. Verse 685 gives the opposite answer to the same demand.

claims.claim: present helplessness is the fruit of deeds undertaken earlier
earlier kings ruled by pleasing the overlord, and that is the precedent

671.reading: Having thought thus, the king looks at the sceptre-bearing sky-goers and tells them that he will gather what is here and send it with them, and bids them carry his courteous word to their lord.
671.nuance: The envoys are called by a name for the sky-goers; taking them to be Asvagriva's Vidyadhara envoys rests on 678 and 680.
671.event: The king tells Asvagriva's envoys he will gather what is due and send it back with them.

672.reading: The king says to himself that the young men will burn if they hear this and that he will send the envoys back at once, and then gives them what they ask by custom.
672.nuance: The young men are taken to be the princes Vijayan and Tivittan; the verse says only that fierce youths would flare at the news.
672.event: The king hides the matter from the princes and gives the envoys what they ask, to send them away quickly.

673.reading: The king calls for the women of the long dark hair, slender-waisted and full-breasted, to come.
673.event: The king summons the dancing women.

674.reading: On hearing the king's grace the women leave the drum, the dance-ground and the songs they were practising and go.
674.event: The women leave their dance practice at the king's word.

675.reading: The women come, bright like a flock of peacocks in a cloud, into the lamp-lit hall, their waists aching under the girdles and their anklets sounding as bees follow them.
675.event: The women arrive in the lit hall.

676.reading: The women, whose singing is like the lute-goddess and whose dancing is like Rambha's, are described, and the king gives a thousand of them away.
676.nuance: The giving is part of the tribute, as 678 shows, where they are put into the flying car with the other gifts; the verse itself says only that he gave them.
676.event: The king gives a thousand of the dancing women to the envoys.

677.reading: The king gives all that pleases the envoys: coral, strings of pearl, tusks and bundles of yak-tail whisks.
677.event: The king gives gems and fine things to the envoys.

678.reading: At the king's leave the Vidyadharas load the gifts into their flying car and put the women in, and the princes see this as the curtain is lowered over it.
678.nuance: The curtain hides the load only as it closes; the princes see the departure and ask in 679.
678.event: The envoys load the gifts and the women into their flying car and the princes see them go.

679.reading: Tivittan asks what has happened and who these messengers are, and all stay silent in fear until a dwarf like a great ghost tells him.
679.nuance: The sea-hued one is taken to be Tivittan, by his colour in the earlier chapters; the verse does not name him.
679.event: Tivittan asks what is happening and a dwarf answers when no one else will.

680.reading: The dwarf says that Asvagriva, lord of the discus whom the earth bows to, sent word that tribute must be given, and that this is what has happened here.
680.event: The dwarf tells Tivittan that Asvagriva has demanded tribute from the king.

681.reading: At the word tribute-duty the anger he has long held in a full heart kindles in him as a fire rising from a grudge.
681.nuance: The subject of the burning is taken to be Tivittan, the prince who asked in 679; 683 later calls him the younger youth.
681.event: Tivittan is lit with anger on hearing the word tribute.

682.reading: His forehead beads with small drops of sweat like pearls dropped from his crown, and his red eyes shed hot tears like ghee falling into the fire.
682.nuance: The verse describes the body's signs of anger and has no event of its own.

683.reading: He looks with the glare of a cobra whose jewelled hood is touched, laughs a fiery laugh and gives the younger one's reply.
683.nuance: The word for the younger youth is read as Tivittan, the younger prince; the line takes up his own reply in 684 to 688.
683.event: Tivittan laughs in anger and answers the demand.

684.reading: Tivittan says that to live by paying written tribute, like men who plough, pay their debts, eat and serve kings, would make a fine royal life.
684.nuance: The tone is scorn: the verse praises what it means to mock. Its claim is set against the king's reasoning in 670.

claims.claim: a king who pays written tribute lives like a tenant, and that is no royal life

685.reading: Tivittan says they would pay tribute daily and rule the land only if their shoulders, their warrior's anklets and their sword were of no use, and asks what use they are otherwise.
685.nuance: The addressee is taken to be Asvagriva's envoys or the deluded people of the court; the verse does not decide which.

claims.claim: a warrior's strength is for refusing tribute, and paying it makes arm and sword useless

686.reading: Tivittan calls the king who demands the tribute a fool who thinks to take the jewel from the hood of a fire-breathing, venom-eyed cobra.
686.nuance: The cobra is Tivittan's own side; the image makes the demander the victim of his own greed.

claims.claim: to demand tribute from a strong man is like taking a jewel from a cobra's hood

687.reading: Tivittan says that whatever the armies of strife have not won in the places that are his could at best be got by women with great vessels.
687.nuance: The verse is compressed and its reading of the third and fourth lines is very uncertain; it is taken as a barb at the women sent as tribute in 676 to 678.

claims.claim: what force cannot win might at most be had in gifts brought by women

688.reading: Tivittan tells the poor ones that they seem to have frightened the weak in the past with the discus from their stronghold, and bids them leave that, live rightly and guard their lives.
688.nuance: The addressees are the envoys or the court; the verse also answers Asvagriva through them. The final plea to live rightly belongs to Tivittan's speech.

claims.claim: those who bully the weak with force should give it up, live rightly and guard their lives

links.note: Kural 380 says nothing is stronger than fate, and that it arrives first even when one devises another course; verse 668 has the king put fate's power to use as the ground of giving way.
links.teaches: The couplet's law of fate is turned by the king into a reason to submit, which the hero rejects in the same chapter.

gains.a: The verse lacks any statement that no counter-plan can outrun fate, which would turn the king's despair from a mood into a rule.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a person who reaches for its truth to excuse giving way, which shows the rule serving as an alibi.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 2030 gives fate's great strength as the sea-girt earth; verse 668 pictures that strength as fate upsetting a city and handing its wealth to others.
links.teaches: A one-line claim that fate's power is the earth is shown as a scene of one city's wealth passing to another.

gains.a: The verse lacks a general statement that fate's power reaches the whole earth, which would make the loss of one city an instance of that law.
gains.b: The verse of the Tirumanthiram lacks an enactment, which the epic gives in a king reasoning that his own city may be taken and given.

links.note: Kural 680 says those with a small domain, afraid of unrest within, bow to the great and take what they are offered; verse 670 has the king bowing on the strength of earlier kings who pleased their overlord.
links.teaches: The king's submission follows the couplet's prudence step by step, so the prince's later refusal is a refusal of that prudence and not of mere cowardice.

gains.a: The verse lacks a stated policy that a small domain bows to the great, which gives the king's reasoning its general standing.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the felt cost of such bowing, which the epic shows in the king's swallowed insult in 666 and his hiding the deal from the princes in 672.

links.note: Naladiyar 33 says the fool grieves when the fruit of past deeds comes, while the wise take it as an old desert crossed; verse 670 accepts the fruit of deeds without grief and answers by paying.
links.teaches: The same calm acceptance of deeds' fruit that the quatrain offers as freedom is here the mood in which a king submits.

gains.a: The verse lacks a way to meet the fruit of deeds without fretting, which the quatrain gives as passing the desert.
gains.b: The quatrain lacks a case where such acceptance becomes political submission, which the king's use of it supplies.

links.note: Verse 670 holds that earlier kings paid and pleased their overlord and that this is the way; verse 685 says that paying tribute would make one's own arms and sword useless.
links.teaches: The same demand draws the king's resigned precedent and the prince's refusal, so one court holds two ideas of what a king is for.

links.note: Verse 304 said that kings of the sea-girt earth, fearing Asvagriva's anger, had paid tribute and sent word; verse 680 brings the same demand to Podanam.
links.teaches: The earlier claim that every king pays Asvagriva becomes a case at Podanam, where it is the prince who first meets it with anger.

links.note: The house-priest foretold in 446 that the youth would come blazing in anger against the discus-lord; verse 681 shows the first blaze, lit by the word tribute.
links.teaches: The prophecy of anger is given its trigger, a single word of demand, so the fire that is foretold is also provoked.

links.note: Kural 894 says a weak man who harms the strong beckons Death with his hand; verse 686 makes the demander, who counts himself strong, the fool who beckons.
links.teaches: Strength is not settled by who sends the demand, and the couplet's rule can be turned against the one who thinks himself the strong party.

gains.a: The verse lacks a rule that harming the stronger is a gesture that summons death, which gives the cobra image its warning.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a case where the apparent strong man is the one deceived about strength, which the epic supplies.

links.note: Purananuru 73 has the fool who ignored a king's strength as a blind man stumbling on a sleeping tiger; verse 686 has the demander as a fool reaching for the jewel in a cobra's hood.
links.teaches: Both pictures make provoking the strong a blind mistake, and the epic moves the blame from stumbling to coveting.

gains.a: The verse lacks the Sangam king's gentler half, that he would give even his life to men who come with courtesy, which makes the cobra's rage a reply to manner.
gains.b: The poem lacks an image in which the fault is covetousness and not mere ignorance, which the jewel in the hood supplies.

source_issues: Verse 679 line 2: a stray space before a dead consonant was repaired in the text.
Verse 681 line 3: a leftover TSCII character was read as a vowel sign and repaired.
Verses 666 to 670: the verses give no speaker; they are taken as the king's thoughts because 671 ends them with he thought thus.
Verses 681 to 688: the prince is not named in these verses; he is taken to be Tivittan from 679.
